advisors # Guide to assistive technology Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - An overview of assistive technology - How to know it’s right for you - Tablets and smart devices: what we will fund - Our Guideline On this page: 1 - An overview of assistive technology 2 - How to know it’s right for you 3 - Tablets and smart devices: what we will fund 4 - Our Guideline ## An overview of assistive technology Assistive technology is equipment or devices that help you do things you can’t do because of your disability. It ranges from low-cost to high-cost and can be bought from a store, modified or custom-made. We fund assistive technology that’s directly related to your disability. Assistive technology can help you do something more easily or safely. It can also help you live more independently. We only fund assistive technology that’s: - directly related to your disability - helpful to work towards your goals - something our rules say

easily or safely. It can also help you live more independently. We only fund assistive technology that’s: - directly related to your disability - helpful to work towards your goals - something our rules say we can fund - supported by evidence. ### What we won’t fund We can’t fund assistive technology that’s: - not related to your disability - more appropriately funded by another government service or another program - common items that everyone needs, like everyday household furniture. Learn more about what assistive technology is. ## How to know it’s right for you It helps to consider what makes assistive technology a reasonable and necessary NDIS support for you. ### Have you received a recommendation? It’s very common for participants to request assistive technology because a health professional recommended it. It’s important to know a recommendation doesn’t guarantee we can fund it. Whether it’s been recommended or not, we still need evidence to decide if we can fund it for you. ### Does it need to be approved

know a recommendation doesn’t guarantee we can fund it. Whether it’s been recommended or not, we still need evidence to decide if we can fund it for you. ### Does it need to be approved and quoted first? There are some kinds of assistive technology you can buy without needing to get advice. You might feel comfortable buying an item if you’ve bought it before, you know it’s less than $1,500 and it’s low-risk . It’s worth asking if you haven’t bought it before and you’re not sure whether you need advice from an assistive technology advisor . Or you could check with your my NDIS contact , plan manager or support coordinator (if you have one). For assistive technology that’s more than $1,500, you need to provide advice from an assistive technology advisor. You need a quote for high-cost assistive technology. ### Is the assistive technology cost effective? We generally fund the standard level of assistive technology you need based on your goals. We’ll fund the most cost-effective item

need a quote for high-cost assistive technology. ### Is the assistive technology cost effective? We generally fund the standard level of assistive technology you need based on your goals. We’ll fund the most cost-effective item if you ask for a more expensive option that achieves the same outcome as a lower cost option. ### Is there evidence it's the best option for you? Information and evidence play a big role in our decision-making process for funding assistive technology. Evidence could come from various sources. These include: - product trials - previous use of assistive technology - research or literature reviews - expert opinions. We typically look for evidence that supports the effectiveness and safety of any recommended assistive technology. If there’s little or no evidence to support it, we may need more information before we can consider it. ## Tablets and smart devices: what we will fund People often ask us if they can use their NDIS plan to buy tablets and smart devices. We have rules about what we

can consider it. ## Tablets and smart devices: what we will fund People often ask us if they can use their NDIS plan to buy tablets and smart devices. We have rules about what we can and can’t fund. A tablet or smart device is a day-to-day household item. This means they’re not usually an NDIS support . ### For some people, a tablet or smart device will be a replacement support Sometimes, we fund smart devices such as tablets as a replacement support . This means we might replace an existing NDIS support in your plan with a tablet. A replacement support must be related to your disability. It replaces a current support in your plan. It isn’t an extra support. You need to apply for a replacement support. You can only buy this support if we approve it in writing. ## Our Guideline Download the assistive technology guideline: - Assistive technology (PDF 291 KB) - Assistive technology (DOCX 104 KB) ## Main navigation sidebar ### For participants -

# Guide to home modifications Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - An overview of home modifications - What we can and can’t fund - Your modification options - Home modifications for new home builds - How they work - Speak to your my NDIS contact - Our Guideline On this page: 1 - An overview of home modifications 2 - What we can and can’t fund 3 - Your modification options 4 - Home modifications for new home builds 5 - How they work 6 - Speak to your my NDIS contact 7 - Our Guideline ## An overview of home modifications Home modifications are updates made to your home to help manage your disability. They can be minor, like installing a new tap or something complex like modifying a bathroom. ### Home modifications are different to assistive technology Assistive technology can be items you buy from a shop and place in your home. Home modifications are parts of your home you change.

modifying a bathroom. ### Home modifications are different to assistive technology Assistive technology can be items you buy from a shop and place in your home. Home modifications are parts of your home you change. For example, the structure or fixtures and fittings. Home modifications can be more challenging to organise because they often involve installers, builders and qualified tradespeople. For example, a non-slip mat is assistive technology. You can buy it from a shop and place it on the ground. But a non-slip floor treatment is a home modification. You ask an installer to come to your home and apply it to the floor. ## What we can and can’t fund Make a list of your goals and how home modifications will help you work towards them before you speak with your my NDIS contact about home modification support. Your my NDIS contact will always consider if your request meets the NDIS supports that relate to your disability when looking at adding home modification supports into your plan. This

contact about home modification support. Your my NDIS contact will always consider if your request meets the NDIS supports that relate to your disability when looking at adding home modification supports into your plan. This means they might ask you questions such as: - Does the home modification relate to your disability? - Will the home modification help you take part in social and work life? - Is the home modification effective and beneficial for you? - Is the home modification legal and safe? - Should the home modification be funded or provided by another service? - Is the home modification value for money? NDIS funding can only pay for modifications to a home you own or to a home the owner agrees can be modified. Your my NDIS contact will tell you what other home and living supports are available if they think home modifications aren’t the best solution for you. Learn more about NDIS home and living options. ## Your modification options ### Simple home adaptions Simple home

home and living supports are available if they think home modifications aren’t the best solution for you. Learn more about NDIS home and living options. ## Your modification options ### Simple home adaptions Simple home adaptions are changes to your home to make it safer and easier to move around. They cost less than $1500 each. They're usually funded as a low-cost assistive technology . ### Minor home modifications Minor home modifications are changes to your home that are straightforward and don’t affect the structure of your home. ### Complex home modifications Complex home modifications are changes to your home that affect its structure and or need custom or more technical work. Learn more about what home modifications are . ## Home modifications for new home builds We can consider funding costs to change standard features of a house design to specific features that meet your disability support needs. Examples we may consider funding include the costs to: - have a wider doorway over a standard doorway - install a disability specific toilet over a standard toilet. Examples we likely wouldn’t fund include the costs: - for extensive earthworks due to choosing a sloping block - to install a stair, platform or vertical lift due to choosing a two-storey house design. ## How they work Your my NDIS contact will talk to you about gathering the evidence you need to apply for funding when you ask for home modifications. text: of assistive technology # What is low-cost assistive technology Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What assistive technology is - What low-cost assistive technology is - What low-cost assistive technology is like On this page: 1 - What assistive technology is 2 - What low-cost assistive technology is 3 - What low-cost assistive technology is like ## What assistive technology is Assistive technology is equipment or a device that helps you complete tasks you might not be able to because of your disability. Assistive technology can help you in many areas of your life, including mobility, leisure and self-care. Having assistive technology can help build your capacity and increase your independence. ## What low-cost assistive technology is Low-cost assistive technology costs less than $1,500. You can usually buy it from a store or online because it doesn’t need to be custom-made or modified. You generally won’t need advice or set up support to start using it safely. Even if the assistive technology is

source_title: What is low-cost assistive technology | NDIS
text: it from a store or online because it doesn’t need to be custom-made or modified. You generally won’t need advice or set up support to start using it safely. Even if the assistive technology is low-cost, you still need to make sure: - it's directly related to your disability - will help you work towards your goals - something our rules say we can fund - it's safe for you to use - it's supported by evidence, for example, a recommendation from your allied health professional. You can buy low-cost assistive technology with your ‘consumables’ budget. You'll need to tell us what types of low-cost assistive technology you might need so we can include it in your plan. When the assistive technology costs less than $1,500 and it's a low-risk item, you don’t need to give us: - quotes - evidence - assessments. You also dont need to ask us for approval before you buy it. Tip: Using low-cost assistive technology for the first time? We suggest everyone gets advice

text: give us: - quotes - evidence - assessments. You also dont need to ask us for approval before you buy it. Tip: Using low-cost assistive technology for the first time? We suggest everyone gets advice before buying assistive technology, even if it’s low-cost. This makes sure the item's right for you. You can speak to an assistive technology advisor who can help you find assistive technology that's value for money and works for you. ## What low-cost assistive technology is like There are many types of low-cost assistive technology. What you need depends on your situation and goals. Some examples include: ### Mobility aids - walking sticks or canes - four-wheeled walker frames - short portable ramps. ### Communication aids - screen magnifiers - text to voice apps. ### Bathing and toileting support items - shower chairs - hand showers - handrails - incontinence alarms. ### Household support items - modified eating utensils - washing line adaptors - talking kitchen scales - adjustable-height chairs. ## Main navigation sidebar ### For

text: For participants - Types of assistive technology # What is mid-cost or high-cost assistive technology Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What mid-cost and high-cost assistive technology is - What mid-cost and high-cost assistive technology is like On this page: 1 - What mid-cost and high-cost assistive technology is 2 - What mid-cost and high-cost assistive technology is like ## What mid-cost and high-cost assistive technology is ### Mid-cost assistive technology costs between $1,500 and $15,000. It's usually more complex than low-cost assistive technology . You need to have it recommended by an assistive technology advisor . You may also need some help to set it up and to learn how to use it safely. Tip: What's an assistive technology advisor? They can be an allied health practitioner, continence nurse, rehabilitation engineer, assistive technology mentor or other qualified practitioner. ### High-cost assistive technology costs more than $15,000. They're complex items that need an assessment from an assistive technology assessor . This helps us

source_title: What is mid-cost or high-cost assistive technology | NDIS
text: continence nurse, rehabilitation engineer, assistive technology mentor or other qualified practitioner. ### High-cost assistive technology costs more than $15,000. They're complex items that need an assessment from an assistive technology assessor . This helps us understand if it meets the NDIS rules. We may ask you to trial or rent it first. This is because we want to hear about your experience with the item before we can include it as an NDIS support in your plan. Tip: What's an assistive technology assessor? They're a suitably qualified allied health professional. They have the experience to support an assessment of the assistive technology item. For example, they can be an occupational therapist, physiotherapist, speech pathologist or rehabilitation engineer. This needs to be an audiologist for specialised hearing products and a qualified prosthetist for prosthetics. ## What mid-cost and high-cost assistive technology is like There are many types of mid-cost and high-cost assistive technology. What you need depends on your situation and goals. There are examples of mid-cost and high-cost assistive technology

advisors # What is assistive technology Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What assistive technology is for - What working with assistive technology is like On this page: 1 - What assistive technology is for 2 - What working with assistive technology is like ## What assistive technology is for Assistive technology can help you do things you can’t do and help you live more independently. For example, screen reading software can help people with low vision to operate a computer more effectively. Assistive technology also helps you do things more safely. For example, a shower chair might help reduce your risk of falling in the shower. It can also reduce your need for other supports over time. ## What working with assistive technology is like ### There's a broad range of assistive technology available Assistive technology can be items like: - non-slip mats - adaptable knives and forks - wheelchairs - powered adjustable beds - a communication device controlled with your eyes

a broad range of assistive technology available Assistive technology can be items like: - non-slip mats - adaptable knives and forks - wheelchairs - powered adjustable beds - a communication device controlled with your eyes - a wheelchair. ### We don’t fund all assistive technologies We only fund assistive technology that’s reasonable and necessary and is an NDIS support . Our funding decision is based on: - your disability-specific needs - your goals - the evidence that supports it - whether it’s more appropriately funded by other sources. ### We also consider the cost and risk The decisions we make about assistive technology depend on cost, risk and evidence. #### How much it costs Assistive technology can be: - low-cost – under $1,500 - mid-cost – from $1,500 to $15,000 - high-cost – more than $15,000. #### What is the risk to you Low-risk assistive technology won’t usually cause harm when used in daily life. They’re readily available items you choose and use safely with very little help from assistive

$15,000. #### What is the risk to you Low-risk assistive technology won’t usually cause harm when used in daily life. They’re readily available items you choose and use safely with very little help from assistive technology advisors. For example, items like non-slip bathmats or adapted cutlery. You can generally buy low-cost and low-risk assistive technology using your consumables budget. Learn how to buy low-cost assistive technology . You’ll need to get advice from an assistive technology advisor or assistive technology assessor to help choose the right higher-risk assistive technology products for your needs. We generally consider items regulated by the Therapeutic Goods Administration in Australia as higher-risk. For example, items like wheelchairs, beds and bed sticks, vehicle modifications, prosthetics or orthotics. We need information about price, evidence and assessments before we can approve high-risk assistive technology. They’re usually a stated support in your NDIS plan and something we talk to you about before your plan reassessment. Learn how to buy mid-cost or high-cost assistive technology . Tip: You can choose

text: - Assistive technology and advisors # What is an assistive technology advisor Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What an assistive technology advisor is - What an assistive technology advisor is for On this page: 1 - What an assistive technology advisor is 2 - What an assistive technology advisor is for ## What an assistive technology advisor is An assistive technology advisor may be an assistive technology assessor or a mentor. Or, your medical practitioner or specialist may have enough experience to provide advice on what you need. Sometimes they’ll refer you to a more experienced assistive technology advisor. For example, an orientation and mobility specialist in the vision sector. An assistive technology mentor is someone with a recognised qualification in assistive technology advice. ## What an assistive technology advisor is for We suggest you get advice before buying or renting any items when we fund assistive technology in your plan. Assistive technology advisors help you: - learn what assistive technology is

source_title: What is an assistive technology advisor | NDIS
text: assistive technology advisor is for We suggest you get advice before buying or renting any items when we fund assistive technology in your plan. Assistive technology advisors help you: - learn what assistive technology is available - choose the best options for your needs - make sure your assistive technology is safe for you - set up and use your assistive technology. Your advisor will give us different evidence, depending on if the items are: - low-cost - mid-cost or high-cost . You’ll need to work with an assistive technology advisor if the items are mid cost. You need an assessor for assessment of high-cost assistive technology. ### Helping you choose a safe and appropriate item An advisor talks with you to understand your needs and goals and make sure the items you’re hoping to buy suit your situation. They’ll also give safety and setup instructions, especially for higher-risk assistive technology. # What are home modifications Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What home modifications are - What home modifications are for - What home modifications are like On this page: 1 - What home modifications are 2 - What home modifications are for 3 - What home modifications are like ## What home modifications are Home modifications are custom-built changes to where you live that help you access and use areas of your home. NDIS funding can only pay for modifications to a home if you own or to a home if the owner agrees it can be modified. ## What home modifications are for You may need home modifications if you: - have safety concerns or difficulty moving around your home - have trouble getting in or using your shower - can’t use or enter the rooms you need to use in your home - have difficulty working towards your goals in your home because of your disability - need changes to

using your shower - can’t use or enter the rooms you need to use in your home - have difficulty working towards your goals in your home because of your disability - need changes to your home so your carers can support you safely. Your my NDIS contact can explain the different home modification options if you’d like them included in your plan. ## What home modifications are like ### They can be minor Minor home modifications are changes to your home that are straightforward and don’t affect the structure of your home. They: - are relatively low risk - generally cost less than $25,000 in total. Examples include: - adding or removing taps - constructing simple ramps - installing non-slip floor treatments - installing lever door handles. ### They can be complex Complex home modifications are changes to your home that affect its structure or need custom or more technical work. - are a higher risk - often impact several areas of the home - generally cost more than

modifications are changes to your home that affect its structure or need custom or more technical work. - are a higher risk - often impact several areas of the home - generally cost more than $25,000 in total - need approvals and certificates of completion. - installing permanent ramps that need building permit approval - installing elevators or lifts - extensive electrical, plumbing or structural work. ### Home modification assessments We need a home modification assessor to recommend what changes are needed to your home. We’ll fund a building construction practitioner to work with you and the home modification assessor to plan the recommended changes if your home modification is complex. We’ll also fund a building works project manager when the modifications are very expensive and involve major structural work. Your project manager must be independent of any of the builders who quote for the work. Tip: You must use qualified tradespeople. We’ll only pay for home modifications completed by tradespeople who are qualified to complete the type of work

independent of any of the builders who quote for the work. Tip: You must use qualified tradespeople. We’ll only pay for home modifications completed by tradespeople who are qualified to complete the type of work you need. For example, builders, plumbers and electricians. ### What we won’t fund We don’t generally fund: - standard furniture, fixtures or fittings including cosmetic finishes like tiles or tapware, which aren’t needed as part of a home modification - swimming pools and spas, including those used for hydrotherapy - modifications that make your house bigger like adding another storey - repairs to pre-existing damage to your home outside the immediate area where you need home modifications - insurance premiums to insure your home after it’s been modified - standard living costs or routine repairs and maintenance that landlords or homeowners are usually responsible for - fixing home modifications that don’t follow Australian standards. ## Main navigation sidebar ### For participants - Creating a plan Expand or collapse sub-menu for Creating a plan - Creating

text: your home # What are home modification assessments Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What home modification assessments are for - What home modification assessments are like On this page: 1 - What home modification assessments are for 2 - What home modification assessments are like ## What home modification assessments are for A home modification assessment recommends changes to your home to meet your disability support needs. We need evidence to help us decide if the changes meet NDIS funding criteria when you ask for home modifications as part of your plan. A home modification assessment is one type of evidence we’ll use to help us decide. ## What home modification assessments are like There are different assessments for minor and complex home modifications. ### Home modification assessors A qualified occupational therapist must complete minor and complex home modification assessments. They’re called a home modification assessor . ### Funding for the assessment We may include some funding in your capacity building supports

source_title: What are home modification assessments | NDIS
text: assessors A qualified occupational therapist must complete minor and complex home modification assessments. They’re called a home modification assessor . ### Funding for the assessment We may include some funding in your capacity building supports to explore what home modifications you need and to get an assessment. ### The information we need The assessment will ask for information about: - how your disability impacts you at home - what home modifications you may need to be more independent - your home. We can only pay for modifications to a home you own or a home if the owner agrees it can be modified. You need to give us written approval from the homeowner or relevant bodies to make changes to your home. For example if you’re renting, we need written approval from your landlord. We also need your consent to discuss the assessment with your chosen provider. ### Additional information for complex home modification assessments You’ll also be asked if you need to hire any facilities or live in another

source_title: What are home modification assessments | NDIS
text: also need your consent to discuss the assessment with your chosen provider. ### Additional information for complex home modification assessments You’ll also be asked if you need to hire any facilities or live in another home while works are underway for a complex home modification assessment. We need 2 itemised quotes for complex home modifications. A building construction practitioner helps to gather these quotes. We’ll also accept a cost estimation done by a qualified building cost estimator or quantity surveyor. ### You can use a template You don’t have to use the template if you don’t want to, but the evidence you provide must include all the information the template asks for. text: - Modifying your home # What is a home modification assessor Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What a home modification assessor is - What a home modification assessor is for - What working with a home modification assessor is like On this page: 1 - What a home modification assessor is 2 - What a home modification assessor is for 3 - What working with a home modification assessor is like ## What a home modification assessor is A home modification assessor is someone who makes recommendations about ways to help you live more independently in your home. They are an occupational therapist with special qualifications and experience. They must have: - professional occupational therapist qualifications and be registered with the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (APRHA) - completed post graduate education and/or training specifically on the assessment, specification and implementation of home modifications. ## What a home modification assessor is for You’ll need to work with a home modification assessor if

source_title: What is a home modification assessor | NDIS
text: - completed post graduate education and/or training specifically on the assessment, specification and implementation of home modifications. ## What a home modification assessor is for You’ll need to work with a home modification assessor if you want minor or complex home modifications . They’ll do a home modification assessment with you for these types of modifications. They’ll ask about your disability support needs at home and certify the effectiveness of the modification to meet your goals. They’ll also consider your likely future needs during planning and on completion of the works. Tip: Looking for a home modification assessor to work with? You can use our provider finder to find a home modification assessor in your area. Your my NDIS contact can also help connect you with a home modification assessor. ## What working with a home modification assessor is like ### Explain the process The assessor will explain the home modification assessment process to you. They’ll explain their role and the approval process. ### Understand your goals and needs The

source_title: What is a home modification assessor | NDIS
text: home modification assessor is like ### Explain the process The assessor will explain the home modification assessment process to you. They’ll explain their role and the approval process. ### Understand your goals and needs The assessor will talk to you about your goals and current NDIS supports. This is so they have a good understanding of what home modifications will help you with your disability support needs and to work towards your goals. They’ll also understand what works best with your other supports. ### Do the assessment at your home The assessor will complete the assessment. They’ll do this with you and ask questions about your needs. They may complete a minor or complex home modification assessment template . ### Provide advice The assessor will explain your options and provide advice on what home modifications will help you with your needs and to work towards your goals. ### Make recommendations The assessor will give us recommendations on the most appropriate home modification option for you. ### Work with builders and

source_title: What is a home modification assessor | NDIS
text: will help you with your needs and to work towards your goals. ### Make recommendations The assessor will give us recommendations on the most appropriate home modification option for you. ### Work with builders and planners, if needed We may be able to provide funding for a building construction practitioner if you need a complex home modification. They’ll work with you and your assessor to help plan the recommended modifications. They can help you with the review and appointment of builders or other suppliers. Building construction practitioners have building knowledge and expertise to: - give advice on the design and cost of home modifications - outline the scope of work - provide drawings so builders can give quotes on the works. We’ll also fund a building works project manager when the modifications are very complex and involve major structural changes to your home. A building works project manager can help find a builder and supervise construction once your complex home modification is approved. Building works project managers have building knowledge

source_title: What is a home modification assessor | NDIS
text: and involve major structural changes to your home. A building works project manager can help find a builder and supervise construction once your complex home modification is approved. Building works project managers have building knowledge and expertise to: - give advice on the builders' qualifications and expertise - make sure the builder delivers the agreed works - help you manage the home modification project. Both the building construction practitioner and the building works project manager should be independent of the builder. You may also need help from other building professionals including architects, engineers and building surveyors. source_title: What is an assistive technology assessor | NDIS
text: - Assistive technology and advisors # What is an assistive technology assessor Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What an assistive technology assessor is - What an assistive technology assessor is for On this page: 1 - What an assistive technology assessor is 2 - What an assistive technology assessor is for ## What an assistive technology assessor is An assistive technology assessor is a specialist assistive technology advisor . They're a health professional who can give you advice and complete an assessment for assistive technology. ### Assistive technology assessors must have special qualifications Assistive technology assessors must: - have relevant qualifications and experience to give you advice about a particular type of assistive technology - have a university or equivalent degree relevant to providing assistive technology assessments - work within the standards set by a professional registration organisation, such as the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency. ### Your health professional can refer you to an assistive technology assessor Not all health professionals

source_title: What is an assistive technology assessor | NDIS
text: - work within the standards set by a professional registration organisation, such as the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency. ### Your health professional can refer you to an assistive technology assessor Not all health professionals have the specialist qualifications to be an assistive technology assessor. Your health professional can refer you to an assistive technology assessor if they can’t complete your assistive technology assessment. This could be a referral to a: - nurse continence specialist - allied health practitioner - orientation and mobility specialist - professional rehabilitation engineer. ## What an assistive technology assessor is for We need evidence to decide if we can fund assistive technology for you. An assessor can help give you advice and do an assessment to get the information we need. The assessment will be different for everyone. It might involve: - a detailed discussion with you - observations in your home and community - trials of different assistive technology devices. The assessor gives detailed recommendations, often including a written report. This helps us consider

text: involve: - a detailed discussion with you - observations in your home and community - trials of different assistive technology devices. The assessor gives detailed recommendations, often including a written report. This helps us consider your request for funding. ### When you need assistive technology advice We suggest you get advice before buying or renting any items when you have assistive technology funding in your NDIS plan. Your medical professional might have enough experience to provide this advice. If not, they can refer you to an assistive technology assessor to help you find assistive technology that suits your needs. text: of assistive technology # What is higher-risk assistive technology Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What higher-risk assistive technology is - What higher-risk assistive technology is for - What higher-risk assistive technology is like - Our Guideline On this page: 1 - What higher-risk assistive technology is 2 - What higher-risk assistive technology is for 3 - What higher-risk assistive technology is like 4 - Our Guideline ## What higher-risk assistive technology is Higher-risk assistive technology is an item, equipment or device that needs specialised advice to buy, set up and use safely. You'll generally need an assessment from an assistive technology advisor or assistive technology assessor to make sure you get the right item for your needs. ### It might be a regulated item Items regulated by the Therapeutic Goods Administration in Australia are considered higher-risk. ### It may cause harm if used incorrectly You could risk injury if higher-risk assistive technology isn’t set up or used safely. Tip: What is low-risk

source_title: What is higher-risk assistive technology | NDIS
text: the Therapeutic Goods Administration in Australia are considered higher-risk. ### It may cause harm if used incorrectly You could risk injury if higher-risk assistive technology isn’t set up or used safely. Tip: What is low-risk assistive technology? Low-risk assistive technology comes with a low risk of harm when used in a daily living environment. You won’t need too much advice or setup support from assistive technology advisors to use them safely. For example, a non-slip bathmat or a shower stool. ## What higher-risk assistive technology is for Higher-risk assistive technology is for equipment that’s: - complex, like a power wheelchair - known to have caused harm - used to restrict voluntary movement, like bed rails or weighted blankets. Examples include: - adjustable beds - bed sticks and other transfer aids - motor vehicle adaptions - complex bathing and toileting devices - pressure care devices - prosthetics or orthotics - devices to support breathing. ## What higher-risk assistive technology is like ### It doesn’t always depend on cost High-cost assistive technology,

source_title: What is higher-risk assistive technology | NDIS
text: complex bathing and toileting devices - pressure care devices - prosthetics or orthotics - devices to support breathing. ## What higher-risk assistive technology is like ### It doesn’t always depend on cost High-cost assistive technology, like a powered wheelchair would be considered higher-risk. Some low-cost items can be higher-risk, like bed poles and weighted blankets. ### Understanding risk You’ll need to know how to use your assistive technology safely and understand any risks. You’ll need written advice to buy or rent higher-risk assistive technology. text: For participants - Assistive technology assessments # What is a general assistive technology assessment Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What a general assistive technology assessment is - What a general assistive technology assessment is for - What a general assistive technology assessment is like On this page: 1 - What a general assistive technology assessment is 2 - What a general assistive technology assessment is for 3 - What a general assistive technology assessment is like ## What a general assistive technology assessment is This assessment collects information from you and your assistive technology advisor . It explains why your plan needs to include assistive technology. The assessment should: - explain how the assistive technology will help you work towards your goals - include information about any previous assistive technology you’ve used - explain how the item will work with your other NDIS supports - include an approximate cost to buy and maintain the item (for mid-cost items) and a quote (for

source_title: What is a general assistive technology assessment | NDIS
text: previous assistive technology you’ve used - explain how the item will work with your other NDIS supports - include an approximate cost to buy and maintain the item (for mid-cost items) and a quote (for high-cost items). If you’ve completed a trial of the assistive technology, please include: - details about how you can safely use the item - the long-term benefits of having the item as one of your NDIS supports. Tip: Who can provide evidence for the assessment? Your advisor can be an allied health practitioner, rehabilitation engineer or other suitably qualified practitioner, depending on the assistive technology you need. ## What a general assistive technology assessment is for We need information and evidence to help us decide if the assistive technology meets NDIS laws and rules. Or if it’s more appropriately funded by other sources. We also need to consider how the assistive technology will be used as part of your overall package of NDIS supports. For example, having assistive technology that helps you shower independently and

source_title: What is a general assistive technology assessment | NDIS
text: by other sources. We also need to consider how the assistive technology will be used as part of your overall package of NDIS supports. For example, having assistive technology that helps you shower independently and safely might mean you need fewer support worker hours to help you bathe. ## What a general assistive technology assessment is like We have a template to guide the assessment and what information we need. Your advisor doesn’t need to use the template if they don’t want to, but the evidence provided must include all the information the template asks for. ### General assistive technology assessment template Download the general assistive technology assessment template: - General assistive technology assessment template (DOCX 78.84KB) ## Main navigation sidebar ### For participants - Creating a plan Expand or collapse sub-menu for Creating a plan - Creating your first plan Expand or collapse sub-menu for Creating your first plan - What is an NDIS plan - Guide to your first plan - Understanding the plan meeting Expand or collapse

text: Reporting fraud - Other support - For participants - Assistive technology assessments # What is a nutrition and dysphagia assistive technology supports assessment Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What a nutrition and dysphagia assistive technology support assessment is - What a nutrition and dysphagia assistive technology support assessment is for - What a nutrition and dysphagia assistive technology support assessment is like On this page: 1 - What a nutrition and dysphagia assistive technology support assessment is 2 - What a nutrition and dysphagia assistive technology support assessment is for 3 - What a nutrition and dysphagia assistive technology support assessment is like ## What a nutrition and dysphagia assistive technology support assessment is The assessment collects information from you and your treating health professional. It describes your situation and explains why your plan needs to include these types of products and supports to help you manage: - food preparation - food substitutes such as oral nutritional supplements - equipment - eating.

source_title: What is a nutrition and dysphagia assistive technology supports assessment | NDIS
text: your situation and explains why your plan needs to include these types of products and supports to help you manage: - food preparation - food substitutes such as oral nutritional supplements - equipment - eating. The assessment should include information about your condition and treatment. It should also include any functional limitations related to your disability that mean you might need some help to manage your condition. The assessment should tell us: - about any assistive technology or products you might have tested - if they've have been beneficial - how they're helping you work towards your NDIS goals. Your treating health professional and assistive technology assessor should tell us about the supports they recommend. They should tell us why and provide evidence to support their suggestions. Tip: Who provides evidence for the assessment? Your evidence can come from different professionals, depending on the NDIS supports you need. We need evidence from: - an assistive technology assessor for assistive technology - a speech pathologist for dysphagia supports - your doctor

source_title: What is a nutrition and dysphagia assistive technology supports assessment | NDIS
text: evidence can come from different professionals, depending on the NDIS supports you need. We need evidence from: - an assistive technology assessor for assistive technology - a speech pathologist for dysphagia supports - your doctor or accredited practising dietitian for nutrition supports. ## What a nutrition and dysphagia assistive technology support assessment is for We can’t fund supports to treat health conditions. The Australian health system provides health services to everyone for illnesses or chronic health conditions. This includes nutrition and dysphagia. We may fund disability-related health supports if you need help to manage your nutrition and eating because of your disability. The assessment helps us decide if we can include these supports in your plan. We need information that shows they're: - related to your disability - a regular part of your daily life - suggested with evidence from your treating health professional - an NDIS support our rules say we can pay for. ## What a nutrition and dysphagia assistive technology support assessment is like We have a

text: For participants - Assistive technology assessments # What is a continence-related assistive technology assessment Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What a continence-related assistive technology assessment is - What a continence-related assistive technology assessment is for - What a continence-related assistive technology assessment is like On this page: 1 - What a continence-related assistive technology assessment is 2 - What a continence-related assistive technology assessment is for 3 - What a continence-related assistive technology assessment is like ## What a continence-related assistive technology assessment is The assessment collects information from you and your treating health professional. It describes your situation and explains why your NDIS plan needs to include continence supports related to your disability. The assessment should include information about your condition and treatment. It should also include any functional limitations related to your disability that mean you might need some help to manage incontinence. The assessment should tell us: - about any assistive technology or products you already use or might

source_title: What is a continence-related assistive technology assessment | NDIS
text: include any functional limitations related to your disability that mean you might need some help to manage incontinence. The assessment should tell us: - about any assistive technology or products you already use or might have tested - how often you use them - how they're helping you work towards your goals. Your treating health professional should tell us about the supports they recommend. They should tell us why and provide evidence to support their suggestions. Tip: Who can provide evidence for the assessment? Your evidence can come from your allied health practitioner or continence nurse. ## What a continence-related assistive technology assessment is for We can’t fund supports to treat health conditions. The Australian health system provides health services to everyone for illnesses or chronic health conditions. This includes continence support services. We may fund disability-related health supports if you need help to manage incontinence because of your disability. The assessment helps us decide if we can include these supports in your plan. When you ask us for these

source_title: What is a continence-related assistive technology assessment | NDIS
text: fund disability-related health supports if you need help to manage incontinence because of your disability. The assessment helps us decide if we can include these supports in your plan. When you ask us for these items, we need information that shows they're: - related to your disability - a regular part of your daily life - suggested with evidence from your treating health professional - an NDIS support our rules say we can pay for. ## What a continence-related assistive technology assessment is like We have a template to guide the assessment and what information we need. You don’t have to use the assessment template, but the evidence you give us must include all the information the template asks for. ### Continence-related assistive technology assessment template Download the continence-related assistive technology assessment template: - Continence-related assistive technology assessment template (DOCX 104KB) ## Main navigation sidebar ### For participants - Creating a plan Expand or collapse sub-menu for Creating a plan - Creating your first plan Expand or collapse sub-menu for

text: - Other support - For participants - Assistive technology assessments # What is a prosthetics and orthotics assistive technology assessment Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What a prosthetics and orthotics assessment is - What a prosthetics and orthotics assessment is for - What a prosthetics and orthotics assessment is like On this page: 1 - What a prosthetics and orthotics assessment is 2 - What a prosthetics and orthotics assessment is for 3 - What a prosthetics and orthotics assessment is like ## What a prosthetics and orthotics assessment is The assessment collects information from you and your assistive technology assessor . It describes your situation and recommends the most suitable and cost-effective prostheses or orthoses to meet your needs and help you work towards your goals. The assessment should include information about assistive technologies or therapies you’ve tried previously and why they did or didn't work for you. It’s important to include information about any clinical trials and professional assessments you’ve

source_title: What is a prosthetics and orthotics assistive technology assessment | NDIS
text: The assessment should include information about assistive technologies or therapies you’ve tried previously and why they did or didn't work for you. It’s important to include information about any clinical trials and professional assessments you’ve completed. It’s also important to include detail about the prostheses or orthoses your treating health professional recommends, such as: - what it’s made of - what components it has (for example, joints) - how much it costs to make and maintain. Tip: What kind of professionals need to provide evidence for the assessment? Your assessor might be an allied health practitioner, such as a prosthetist or orthotist, or a medical or clinical professional who specialises in limb assessments, depending on your situation. ## What a prosthetics and orthotics assessment is for We need information and evidence to help us decide about the right prostheses or orthoses for you. We’ll generally provide funding for the most cost-effective prostheses or orthoses. This means we’ll first look at items with the minimum necessary components to meet your needs

source_title: What is a prosthetics and orthotics assistive technology assessment | NDIS
text: about the right prostheses or orthoses for you. We’ll generally provide funding for the most cost-effective prostheses or orthoses. This means we’ll first look at items with the minimum necessary components to meet your needs and support you to work towards your goals. We’ll need information and evidence that shows you’ve tested the lower cost option and explains why it isn’t suitable for you if you'd like us to consider a more expensive option. We also need to understand: - why the more expensive option will benefit you in the longer term - how it'll increase your independence - how it'll build your capacity - how it'll reduce the other NDIS supports in your plan, like personal care supports. ## What a prosthetics and orthotics assessment is like We have a template to guide the assessment and what information we need. You don’t have to use the prosthetics and orthotics assessment template if you don’t want to, but the evidence you give us must include all the information the template

text: - How to buy or rent assistive technology # How to buy low-cost assistive technology Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - Step 1: Check your plan - Step 2: Find a provider - Step 3: Make a claim On this page: 1 - Step 1: Check your plan 2 - Step 2: Find a provider 3 - Step 3: Make a claim ## Step 1: Check your plan ### Make sure you’ve got enough available funding Your funding for low-cost assistive technology will be in your core budget under ‘consumables’. Low-cost assistive technology are any items under $1,500 that are NDIS supports . Learn more about low-cost assistive technology . #### Check you’ve got enough funds to make your purchase Log in to the participant portals or my NDIS app to check your funding balance. You can also ask someone who helps you with your plan, to check for you. You can start the process of buying your low-cost assistive technology if you

source_title: How to buy low-cost assistive technology | NDIS
text: NDIS app to check your funding balance. You can also ask someone who helps you with your plan, to check for you. You can start the process of buying your low-cost assistive technology if you have funds available. You don’t need to check with us first or send us a quote for approval if you have funds in your consumables budget and your assistive technology costs less than $1,500. You’ll need to get advice to make sure it’s safe for you to use if the item you want is higher-risk. ### If you don’t have enough funding You can choose to use your core supports category funding flexibly to buy your low-cost assistive technology if you don’t have enough funding in your ‘consumables’ budget. We can discuss other options with you if you don’t have flexible funding available. This might include doing a plan variation . ## Step 2: Find a provider ### If you’re NDIA-managed You’ll need to buy your item from a registered NDIS provider. You can use

source_title: How to buy low-cost assistive technology | NDIS
text: flexible funding available. This might include doing a plan variation . ## Step 2: Find a provider ### If you’re NDIA-managed You’ll need to buy your item from a registered NDIS provider. You can use our provider finder to help you find one. ### If you’re plan-managed or self-managed You can buy from any supplier. ## Step 3: Make a claim Your registered provider will claim payment for the item directly from us when you buy your low-cost assistive technology. ### If you’re plan-managed You’ll need to give your plan manager the invoice and any required documentation. They’ll handle the payment and claims process on your behalf. ### If you’re self-managed You can pay for your assistive technology upfront then submit a claim for reimbursement through the my NDIS portal , myplace portal or my NDIS app . Tip: Keep your receipts Make sure to keep receipts and any documentation related to your purchase. You’ll need to be able to provide proof of your claim if you’re self-managed. ## Main

text: support - For participants - How to buy or rent assistive technology # How to buy mid-cost or high-cost assistive technology Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - Step 1: Know the cost of the assistive technology you want to buy - Step 2: Get an assessment and information about price - Step 3: Buy your item - Step 4: Make a claim On this page: 1 - Step 1: Know the cost of the assistive technology you want to buy 2 - Step 2: Get an assessment and information about price 3 - Step 3: Buy your item 4 - Step 4: Make a claim ## Step 1: Know the cost of the assistive technology you want to buy We describe assistive technology as low-cost, mid-cost or high-cost. ### Low-cost assistive technology Under $1,500 per item. ### Mid-cost assistive technology Between $1,500 and $15,000 per item. ### High-cost assistive technology Over $15,000 per item. Tip: Buying low-cost assistive technology? Learn more about how

source_title: How to buy mid-cost or high-cost assistive technology | NDIS
text: ### Low-cost assistive technology Under $1,500 per item. ### Mid-cost assistive technology Between $1,500 and $15,000 per item. ### High-cost assistive technology Over $15,000 per item. Tip: Buying low-cost assistive technology? Learn more about how to buy low-cost assistive technology . ## Step 2: Get an assessment and information about price ### Evidence for mid-cost assistive technology You’ll need to give us evidence to show the mid-cost assistive technology you want to buy is right for you. This evidence can be a letter, email or report from your allied health practitioner or other assistive technology advisor you work with. It doesn’t need to be a formal assessment but it does need to be in writing so we can keep it for our records. This evidence should tell us: - the type of assistive technology you need - why it’s the best value to help with your disability support needs over other supports - how it’ll help you work towards the goals in your plan - an estimate of how much

source_title: How to buy mid-cost or high-cost assistive technology | NDIS
text: need - why it’s the best value to help with your disability support needs over other supports - how it’ll help you work towards the goals in your plan - an estimate of how much it costs. ### Evidence for high-cost assistive technology You’ll need to provide us with an assessment report from a qualified assistive technology assessor if the assistive technology is more than $15,000. This report needs to shows what assistive technology you need. You can use our provider finder to help you find a qualified assistive technology assessor. ### Get a quote for high-cost assistive technology You’ll need to provide us with a quote if your item costs more than $15,000. Make sure the quote includes delivery, installation and any training costs. You usually need to give us one quote. Sometimes we might need a second quote to check your assistive technology is value for money. ### Make sure high-cost assistive technology is right for you You might need to trial the assistive technology before you know

source_title: How to buy mid-cost or high-cost assistive technology | NDIS
text: might need a second quote to check your assistive technology is value for money. ### Make sure high-cost assistive technology is right for you You might need to trial the assistive technology before you know it’s right for you. When you need to try the assistive technology first, we will include funds in your capital budget to pay for the trial. ### Send us your evidence Once you’ve gathered your evidence you can share it with us by: - calling us on 1800 800 110 - send an enquiry using the service hub - giving it to your my NDIS contact or delivering it to an office . #### Next steps We’ll add funding to your plan if it’s approved. You can then buy your item. ## Step 3: Buy your item ### If you’re NDIA-managed You’ll need to buy your item from a registered NDIS provider. You can use our provider finder to help you find one. ### If you’re plan-managed or self-managed You can buy from any supplier.

source_title: How to buy mid-cost or high-cost assistive technology | NDIS
text: NDIA-managed You’ll need to buy your item from a registered NDIS provider. You can use our provider finder to help you find one. ### If you’re plan-managed or self-managed You can buy from any supplier. This gives you more flexibility to find what you need from a wider range of products. Tip: Choose to rent your assistive technology. You don’t have to buy your assistive technology outright if you don’t want to. You can also access what you need through rental, loan, subscription or other arrangements. Learn more about how to fund a rental for assistive technology . ## Step 4: Make a claim Your assistive technology provider will claim payment for the item directly from us. ### If you’re plan-managed You’ll need to give your plan manager the invoice for the item, as well as any other required documentation. They’ll handle the payment and claims process on your behalf. ### If you’re self-managed You can pay for your assistive technology upfront, then submit a claim through the participant portal

source_title: How to buy mid-cost or high-cost assistive technology | NDIS
text: as any other required documentation. They’ll handle the payment and claims process on your behalf. ### If you’re self-managed You can pay for your assistive technology upfront, then submit a claim through the participant portal or my NDIS app . Tip: Keep your receipts. Make sure to keep receipts and any documentation related to your purchase. text: 6: Contact us 7 - Step 7: Get the item 8 - Get help or set up advice ## Step 1: Know when it’s best to rent assistive technology You may find it better to rent an assistive technology item when: - it’s for a child, if they are likely to outgrow the technology in a short period of time - your needs are changing quickly - you only need the item for a short period of time, for example, you're waiting for a repair of your regular item or you’re waiting on a new or replacement item - you want to trial an item for an extended period, before deciding if it’s right for you - renting is better value for money than buying the item. Tip: Think you might need to rent mid to high-cost assistive technology? Your NDIA planner can include funding in your capacity building improved daily living budget to get advice from an assistive technology adviser and to prepare an assessment report. ## Step 2:

Your NDIA planner can include funding in your capacity building improved daily living budget to get advice from an assistive technology adviser and to prepare an assessment report. ## Step 2: Decide what item you want to rent ### Work with your assistive technology adviser It’s best to start by talking to an assistive technology advisor to find the right piece of assistive technology for you. Tip: Choosing the right assistive technology advisor. Your assistive technology advisor will have the right qualifications to assess your needs. For example, your adviser will be an audiologist if you need assistive technology for your hearing. Your adviser might be an occupational therapist or physiotherapist if you need assistive technology to move around more easily. ## Step 3: Check the funding in your plan You may have some rental funding included in your plan, if you already use assistive technology. Rental funding in your plan can be found in your assistive technology – maintenance, repair and rental budget. ## Step

Rental funding in your plan can be found in your assistive technology – maintenance, repair and rental budget. ## Step 4: Gather evidence ### Let us know why you need to rent assistive technology Your assistive technology advisor needs to give you written advice that tells us: - what type of item you need to rent - why you need to rent the item - how the item will help with your disability support needs - how long you’ll need to rent it for - how renting the item is the best value way to help you pursue your goals - how much the item might cost to rent. A cost estimate is appropriate for items under $15,000. #### High-cost assistive technology You’ll need to show us a quote and an assessment from an assistive technology assessor if the item you wish to rent costs more than $15,000. ## Step 5: Find a provider ###

text: assistive technology You’ll need to show us a quote and an assessment from an assistive technology assessor if the item you wish to rent costs more than $15,000. ## Step 5: Find a provider ### Talk to a provider about what you need You can choose the provider you want to supply your rental item. You can use our provider finder to find a provider. You can also ask questions about rental items or research providers online. An assistive technology assessor can also help you find providers that might have the items you want to rent. You can talk to providers about the items they have to suit your needs and anything you need to know about using the item. You should also ask about their rental policy. You may need a quote. The provider you choose should be able to give you one. You can sometimes get rental assistive technology through a subscription service if your needs are changing quickly. Your NDIS funding could be NDIA-managed, so you’ll need to use a registered NDIS provider. You can rent from any supplier, if you’re plan-managed. ## Step 6: Contact us #### How to tell us You may need rental funding added to your plan, gather your evidence and quote (if you need one), and: - give it to your my NDIS contact - call us on 1800 800 110 - send an enquiry using our service hub - upload your advice to the NDIS myplace participant portal - bring the information to your check-in or plan meeting . We can put funding to rent it in your capital – assistive technology budget, once we approve the technology budget. ## Step 7: Get the item You can contact your chosen provider and arrange to rent the assistive technology, once you have the funding in your plan. You might get asked to sign an agreement to rent the item from a provider. You need to make sure you’re comfortable with terms and conditions of this agreement, so it’s a good idea to check them. Rental equipment will need to go back to the supplier at the end of the rental agreement. We ask you to sometimes trial high-cost assistive technology if you haven’t used the item before so we can consider adding funding to your plan to buy it. Tip: Think you might need mid-cost to high-cost assistive technology? Your NDIA planner can include funding in your capacity building improved daily living budget to seek advice from an assistive technology advisor or to prepare an assessment. ## Step 2: Decide what item you want to trial ### Work with your assistive technology advisor It’s best to start by talking to an assistive technology advisor to find out about the right piece of assistive technology for you. Assistive technology advisors are

source_title: How to trial assistive technology | NDIS
text: trial ### Work with your assistive technology advisor It’s best to start by talking to an assistive technology advisor to find out about the right piece of assistive technology for you. Assistive technology advisors are usually allied health practitioners. They give you independent advice to help you choose a safe and appropriate item. Tip: Choosing the right assistive technology advisor. Your assistive technology adviser will have the right qualifications to assess your needs. For example, if you need assistive technology for your hearing, your adviser will be an audiologist. Your adviser might be an occupational therapist or physiotherapist if you need assistive technology to help with your mobility. ## Step 3: Check the funding in your plan You may have some rental funding in your plan that can be used to fund a short trial if you already use assistive technology. You can find rental funding in your assistive technology – maintenance, repair and rental budget. ## Step 4: Gather evidence ### Let us know why you need to trial

text: if you already use assistive technology. You can find rental funding in your assistive technology – maintenance, repair and rental budget. ## Step 4: Gather evidence ### Let us know why you need to trial assistive technology #### Mid-cost assistive technology You don't need to show us a quote if the item costs between $1,500 and $15,000. But you do need to give us written advice from your assistive technology adviser that tells us: - what type of item you need to trial - why you need to trial the item - how the item will help with your disability support needs - how long you'll need to trial it for - how much the item might cost to trial. #### Guide for minor trial and rental funding Our guide for minor trial and rental funding gives information on how much we can fund for mid-cost item trials. Download the guide for minor trial and rental funding: - Guide for minor trial and rental funding (DOCX 61KB) #### High-cost assistive

source_title: How to trial assistive technology | NDIS

Download the guide for minor trial and rental funding: - Guide for minor trial and rental funding (DOCX 61KB) #### High-cost assistive technology You’ll need to give us a quote and an assessment from an assistive technology assessor if the item you want to trial costs more than $15,000 and is high-cost to rent. ## Step 5: Find a provider ### Ask the provider how a trial works You can choose the provider you want to supply your trial item. Use our provider finder to research providers online or get information about trial items. Ask your assistive technology advisor to help you choose providers that might have the items you want to trial. Talk to providers about the items they have to suit your needs and anything you need to know about using the item. It’s also a good idea to ask about any terms and conditions they have for trialling the item. Some providers offer ’trial

text: suit your needs and anything you need to know about using the item. It’s also a good idea to ask about any terms and conditions they have for trialling the item. Some providers offer ’trial to buy’ arrangements. You can ask the provider if the cost of a trial will be taken off the price if you buy the item after your trial. ## Step 6: Contact us ### How to tell us Gather your evidence and quote (if you need one) if you need funding added to your plan and: - give it to your my NDIS contact - call us on 1800 800 110 - enquire through our service hub - upload your advice to the participant portal - bring the information to your check-in or plan meeting . Once we approve the item and what it costs, we can put funding to trial it in your capital – assistive technology budget. ## Step 7: Get the item and trial it Contact your assistive technology advisor and your

text: item and what it costs, we can put funding to trial it in your capital – assistive technology budget. ## Step 7: Get the item and trial it Contact your assistive technology advisor and your chosen supplier to get the assistive technology item delivered for trial once the funding is in your plan. ### Get help Your assistive technology item might involve a complicated set-up process. Ask your assistive technology advisor for help. ## Step 8: Decide if you want to buy it ### If the item is right for you Ask your assistive technology advisor for help to work out if a mid-cost assistive technology item is right for you. They can provide you with a letter or report that supports you buying the item. Keep this document for your records. You can buy mid-cost assistive technology item if you already have funding in your plan. Your assistive technology assessor will need to complete a general assistive technology assessment if the item is a high-cost item. They’ll need to

source_title: How to trial assistive technology | NDIS
text: mid-cost assistive technology item if you already have funding in your plan. Your assistive technology assessor will need to complete a general assistive technology assessment if the item is a high-cost item. They’ll need to give the assessment and a quote for the item to us. We’ll then consider funding the item. ### If the item isn't right for you Contact the provider to organise the item’s return if it doesn’t suit you and your situation. text: your vehicle # What is a vehicle modification Listen Print this page Save page as PDF ### On this page: - What a vehicle modification is - What a vehicle modification is for - How vehicle modifications work - Our Guideline On this page: 1 - What a vehicle modification is 2 - What a vehicle modification is for 3 - How vehicle modifications work 4 - Our Guideline ## What a vehicle modification is You may need changes made to a vehicle so you can drive it or travel in it. We call these changes vehicle modifications. Vehicle modifications can be changes to a car or other type of vehicle you or your family use for your transport. Modifications make sure you can drive the vehicle or be a passenger in the vehicle. Some common modifications include: - wheelchair passenger ramps and wheelchair hoists - modified driving controls - modified restraints and modified car seats. ## What a vehicle modification is for ### Modifications funded because of your disability

source_title: What is a vehicle modification | NDIS
text: common modifications include: - wheelchair passenger ramps and wheelchair hoists - modified driving controls - modified restraints and modified car seats. ## What a vehicle modification is for ### Modifications funded because of your disability You might be able to get NDIS funding for vehicle modification and driving supports to help you: - become as independent as possible when you travel - travel safely to work or activities. In addition to funding modifications to your vehicle, you may also be able to have NDIS funding in your plan for: - assessing your need for a vehicle modification - extra insurance costs because of your modified vehicle - maintenance or repairs of your vehicle modification - help with transport while your vehicle is modified. ### Vehicle ownership You or your family need to own a vehicle that is suitable to modify or have found a suitable vehicle you plan to purchase or lease. You should get advice from an occupational therapist with experience in vehicle modifications if you’re going to purchase

source_title: What is a vehicle modification | NDIS
text: that is suitable to modify or have found a suitable vehicle you plan to purchase or lease. You should get advice from an occupational therapist with experience in vehicle modifications if you’re going to purchase a vehicle to modify. This’ll make sure you buy the right type of vehicle that can be modified for your needs. You need permission from the vehicle owner to modify their vehicle and be able to use it most of the time if you don’t own the vehicle. ### Specialised driver training may also be funded We may also fund a specialised vehicle driving instructor for extra lessons you might need: - because of your disability - to learn how to use the modifications in your vehicle. ### What we don’t fund Our rules say what we can fund. Under NDIS rules, we can’t fund things relating to your vehicle like: - buying or leasing a vehicle - registration - insurance - running costs, like petrol, servicing or repairs - driving lessons to get your

source_title: What is a vehicle modification | NDIS
text: NDIS rules, we can’t fund things relating to your vehicle like: - buying or leasing a vehicle - registration - insurance - running costs, like petrol, servicing or repairs - driving lessons to get your driver’s licence. ## How vehicle modifications work We can only include NDIS supports in your plan if they meet all the NDIS funding criteria. We consider your request for vehicle modification funding if it’s: - a support NDIS funds - related to your disability - going to help you work towards your goals - effective and beneficial for you - value for money - legal and safe. We review your vehicle modifications together with all your transport needs to decide the best funded supports for your circumstances. Funding for vehicle modifications may reduce your need for other supports, for example transport funding. ### Talk to your my NDIS contact or health professional You can ask for this funding in your NDIS plan if you think a modified vehicle may help you. We need evidence or

source_title: What is a vehicle modification | NDIS
text: transport funding. ### Talk to your my NDIS contact or health professional You can ask for this funding in your NDIS plan if you think a modified vehicle may help you. We need evidence or an assessment to decide if we’ll include funding to explore vehicle modification options in your plan. This usually comes from your allied health provider and medical practitioner (GP) and tells us about your need for modified transport. The best way to start this process is to talk to your my NDIS contact or your treating health professional. source_title: How to get a vehicle modified | NDIS
text: modifications ## Step 1: Get advice from an occupational therapist We may fund modifications to a vehicle so you can drive it or travel in it. When considering if we will fund a vehicle modification, we look at if the vehicle modifications and driving supports: - are needed because of your disability - will help you work towards your goals - are NDIS supports . An occupational therapist can give you advice about vehicle modifications. Tip: We can’t fund the purchase of a vehicle It’s important to know we can’t fund the purchase of a vehicle to modify. ## Step 2: Gather your evidence for your planning meeting #### For drivers: get a report from your doctor Your doctor must check you’re fit to drive using the national Assessing Fitness to Drive medical standards if you’re planning to drive a modified vehicle. The report should also outline your need for modified transport. We can decide if we’ll include funding in your plan for an assessment to explore your driving options

text: you’re planning to drive a modified vehicle. The report should also outline your need for modified transport. We can decide if we’ll include funding in your plan for an assessment to explore your driving options when we receive the report. #### When you’re a passenger Ask your NDIA planner at your planning meeting to include funding for a vehicle modification assessment with an occupational therapist, if you’re a passenger, or a parent or carer who needs to modify their vehicle. ## Step 3: Use your funding to get an assessment ### Talk to an occupational therapist #### If you’re the one driving We need an assessment from a driver-trained occupational therapist if you want to drive the vehicle. Use our provider finder to look for one or talk to your my NDIS contact or support coordinator , if you have one. text: coordinator , if you have one. We have a vehicle modification assessment template your driver trained occupational therapist can complete to give us all the information about the assessment. This evidence should tell us what modifications you’re asking for. For a second-hand, already modified vehicle, the evidence should confirm the modifications are safe for you and suit your current and future needs. Download the vehicle modification assessment template: - Vehicle modification assessment template (DOCX 92KB) #### If you’re a passenger We need an assessment from an occupational therapist to understand what changes are needed to your vehicle to travel in it safely if you’re not driving. We’ll also need to know if you: - own the vehicle - plan to buy or lease the vehicle. You must tell us in writing if you don’t own the vehicle and if: - its owner agrees to the modifications to it - you can use the vehicle for your transport needs. #### Mid and high-cost modifications Before you arrange for modifications to be

text: NDIA, GPO Box 700, Canberra ACT 2601. ### Deliver it in person You can deliver it to your my NDIS contact. Tip: Having a vehicle modified may reduce your other supports. We look at vehicle modifications along with all your transport needs. For example, it might reduce your transport funding for things like accessible taxis if we fund modifications to a vehicle. ### If your vehicle modifications cost less than $15,000 You can follow our process for buying mid-cost assistive technology . ### If your vehicle modifications cost more than $15,000 You’ll need to send us a quote to approve before you modify your vehicle. ## Step 5: Getting your vehicle modified You can contact the vehicle modifier to arrange a time for your modifications to be done after you have funding for vehicle modifications put in your plan. ### We don’t fund running costs or optional extras.
